turns.doctor_question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response: Well, I'm here because... well, it's been going on for nearly two years now. I'm absolutely sure the contractor we hired and some of the people on my block have been quietly working together to cheat us. They're keeping my kitchen half-wrong on purpose. And you know, kitchens are so important. I remember when I was a little girl, my mother's kitchen was the heart of the house. She had this beautiful yellow wallpaper with little roosters on it. I always wanted a kitchen like that, warm and inviting. But anyway, no matter how many receipts my husband shows me, or how many excuses they all give, I know what they're doing. They think I don't see it, but I do. My husband, bless him, he just doesn't understand. He bought me this lovely set of mixing bowls for my birthday last year, blue ceramic, just gorgeous, but I can't even enjoy using them in that kitchen. They're all in on it, I just know it.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, persecutory belief that her contractor and neighbors are conspiring against her, which she maintains despite her husband showing her contradictory evidence (receipts).

Protecting it from the mailman, I suppose! The mailman we have now is always running late, too. Not like Mr. Henderson from when my kids were little. You could set your watch by Mr. Henderson. The blue jays absolutely loved it, but the squirrels, oh my goodness, the squirrels would just hang upside down and steal all the suet. We tried everything to keep them away—greasing the pole, putting little baffles on it—but those creatures are like acrobats. I saw a special on PBS once about how smart squirrels actually are, they can solve puzzles and remember where they hid nuts for months. Isn't that incredible? I can barely remember where I put my reading glasses half the time! I had a lovely pair with little rhinestones on the corners, but I left them at the grocery store checkout last Tuesday. The cashier was a new girl, very sweet, but she bagged my bread under a heavy bottle of laundry detergent. It was completely squished by the time I got home. turns.doctor_question: Have you been diagnosed with any brain or neurological illness?
turns.patient_response: Brain illness? No, no, I've never had anything wrong with my brain. Thank goodness for that. My memory is sharp as a tack, except for the reading glasses, of course. It was a very nice facility, they had a beautiful garden with these big, blooming hydrangea bushes. I've always wanted to grow hydrangeas, but the soil in our yard is just too acidic. I read in a magazine—Better Homes and Gardens, I think it was, or maybe Southern Living—that you can change the color of the blooms by putting coffee grounds or rusty nails in the dirt. Isn't that funny? Rusty nails! Arthur used to keep coffee cans full of rusty nails and screws in the garage. He never threw anything away, said you never know when you might need a two-inch wood screw. When we finally cleaned out the garage last spring, we found things we hadn't seen since 1990. We even found the old croquet set we used to play with on the Fourth of July. The kids would get so competitive, especially my son, David. He always had to have the blue mallet. He was so particular, even as a little boy. He wouldn't eat his peas if they touched his mashed potatoes. I had to buy those special plates with the little dividers in them. But no, no brain problems for me. Just regular doctor checkups, that's all.

turns.doctor_question: Do you believe anyone is controlling your thoughts?
turns.patient_response: Controlling my thoughts? Goodness, no, nobody can do that. That sounds like something out of one of those science fiction movies my grandson likes to watch. He came over last weekend and had me sit through this whole film about people living in a computer simulation. It was so loud, all explosions and flashing lights. I told him, "Tommy, my ears are ringing!" He just laughed. He's such a sweet boy, though. He's starting college in the fall, going all the way up to State. I can hardly believe it. It feels like just yesterday he was running around the backyard catching fireflies in a mason jar. We used to poke holes in the lid with an ice pick so they could breathe. You have to be so careful with an ice pick, Arthur always warned me about that. He had an uncle who actually punctured his own hand trying to chip ice for a punch bowl back in the fifties. Can you imagine? They didn't have those fancy refrigerators with the ice makers built right into the door back then. My neighbor, Susan, just remodeled her kitchen and she got one of those refrigerators. Stainless steel, she calls it, but I swear it shows every single fingerprint. I told her, "Susan, you're going to be wiping that thing down three times a day." She's always cleaning, that woman. I think she vacuums her driveway. But no, nobody is putting thoughts in my head or controlling them or anything silly like that. My thoughts are my own.

His office always smelled like peppermint, he kept a bowl of those little red and white striped candies on his desk. The ones wrapped in clear plastic? We used to have pot roast every Sunday, with carrots and potatoes roasted right in the pan juices. I'd make a gravy from scratch, none of that powdered stuff from a packet. I saw a commercial the other day for a machine that makes a whole cup of coffee in thirty seconds. Thirty seconds! Where's the joy in that? I still use my old percolator. It makes this wonderful bubbling sound in the morning, it's so comforting. But no, to answer your question, I haven't started any new medications. Just the same old routine.

You had to take the battery out, and I couldn't reach it! I had to stand on a kitchen chair, and I was waving a dish towel at it like a madwoman. Whenever there was a thunderstorm, he'd hide under the bed and wouldn't come out for hours. I used to have to coax him out with little pieces of cheese. He loved sharp cheddar. 

But anyway, no, nobody has said I stop making sense. I think I make perfect sense, I just have a lot to say sometimes.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient explicitly denies having jumbled thoughts or being told that they stop making sense when talking.

turns.doctor_question: Has anyone who knows you well ever said that your thinking has become disorganized?
turns.patient_response:
Disorganized? Oh, certainly not my thinking. Now, if you want to talk about disorganized, you should have seen my hall closet last weekend! I finally decided to tackle it, and oh my goodness, it was a complete disaster area. I pulled out things I haven't seen in years. I found our old Scrabble board tucked right at the very back under a pile of heavy winter coats. 

We used to play Scrabble every single Sunday evening when the kids were little. My husband always insisted on keeping score, he was very particular about the math. He used this little green spiral notebook. I actually found that notebook, too! It had a grocery list tucked inside from... oh, it must have been 1992. Bread was so much cheaper back then. I usually buy the whole wheat kind now, the one with the little oats baked right onto the crust. It makes the most wonderful toast. I have a slice every morning with my tea and a bit of orange marmalade. I tried making my own marmalade from scratch once, but boiling the rinds takes simply forever and it just made the entire kitchen sticky. My slippers were practically glued to the linoleum! So now I just buy the glass jar with the little gingham lid at the supermarket. It's much easier. 

But no, nobody has ever told me my thinking is disorganized. I keep everything perfectly straight up here.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient explicitly denies having disorganized thinking, but her actual response demonstrates clear tangentiality and loose associations, wandering from a closet to Scrabble, bread, and marmalade.
